newsitem.title: USA: USDA FY98 budget built on November crop outlook.
newsitem.headline: USDA FY98 budget built on November crop outlook.

text.p: The fiscal 1998 budget proposed for the Agriculture Department included four-month old assumptions of large U.S. crops that already have been brought into question for wheat, USDA officials said Thursday.
Based on November 1996 conditions, the projections assumed plantings of 81.5 million acres of corn, 64 million acres of soybeans and 72 million acres of wheat.
Harvest was projected as 9.625 billion bushels of corn, 2.42 billion bushels of soybeans and 2.345 billion bushels of wheat.
Updated figures will be released later this month.

USDA chief economist Keith Collins said new figures, based on current conditions, would be released as part of the USDA Outlook Forum on February 24 and 25. He noted that the wheat acreage number was projected before a December report that put winter wheat acreage at 48.2 million acres, the lowest since 1978. Winter wheat is the major U.S. wheat variety.

Early this week, the U.S. Feed Grains Council forecast 1997 U.S. plantings at 80.7 million acres of corn, 64.1 million acres of soybeans and 72.8 million acres of wheat. Harvest would be 9.49 billion bushels of corn, 2.38 billion bushels of soybeans and 2.449 billion bushels of wheat, it said.
The Feed Grains Council's figures were based on conditions at years' end.

In its projections, the USDA put the average price for 1997 corn at $2.45 a bushel and soybeans at $6.10 a bushel. Its January supply-demand report said the season-average farm-gate price for 1996 corn would be $2.55-2.85 a bushel and for soybeans $6.60-$7.10 a bushel.
At mid-January, analysts, as well as Collins, said they expected corn acreage of around 80 million acres and soybean plantings of 64 million acres, or a bit more.
In 1996, U.S. farmers planted 75.6 million acres of wheat, 79.5 million acres of corn and 64.2 million acres of soybeans.
The decline in winter wheat seedings suggested an overall decline in wheat sowings. Farmers sowed 52 million acres of winter wheat for 1996 harvest.
Half of the drop in winter wheat seedings came in seven Midwestern states where corn and soybeans are dominant crops.
